docs.title: Crosswork CNC Hands-on
docs.text:
This is the operator lab for Cisco Crosswork Network Controller (CNC) 7.2.0. You will use the dCloud session from chapter 1: one CNC, a five-node IOS-XR lab, and a dedicated SR-PCE lab.

Each chapter has an objective, the clicks or CLI, the result you should see, and a short Done when list. Router work in this lab is show output unless a chapter says otherwise. Configuration changes go through CNC.

docs.title: Lab story
docs.text:
1. Bring CNC out of maintenance and start both CML labs.
  2. Confirm CNC, the providers, and collection are healthy.
  3. Read the topology in the UI and confirm it from XR CLI.
  4. Walk inventory, faults, configuration, and performance.
  5. Observe a PCC-initiated SR policy, then create a PCE-initiated SRv6 policy.
  6. Provision an L3VPN and steer it onto that policy.
  7. Provision a VPWS L2VPN. VPLS, an NSO custom template, and sync-from are optional.
  8. Enable Service Health on the VPWS you created.
  9. Collect showtech, read collection jobs and alarms, and walk the patch screen.
  10. Optional: ask the CNC MCP assistant one inventory question.

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
Time: 50 minutes

Objective: Access dCloud environment, leave maintenance mode, start the CML lab, and log in to a controller that is ready for work.

Instructor

Maintenance mode shuts the applications down gracefully, and bringing them back takes several minutes.

docs.title: 1.1 Lab setup and CNC
docs.text:
The lab setup In this scenario, following is the lab setup.

  • CNC version 7.2.0 Single VM
  • P and PE routers: C8000 on CML
  • PCE: XRv9k

For P and PE routers, Cisco 8000 hardware emulator on CML is used. For more information about Cisco 8000 hardware emulator, please refer to following:

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/iosxr/cisco8000-emulator/cisco8000-hardware-emulator-installation-guide.pdf.

XRv9 for PCE is running in a difference CML instance, connected by multiple external connectors.

The difference between Single VM (SVM) and cluster There are two types of CNC deployment: Single VM (SVM) and cluster. In Single VM, all nodes, NSO and Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG) are in single VM. In cluster deployment, each component must be set up as a separate VM.

docs.title: 1.2 Disable maintenance mode
docs.text:
Use maintenance mode to temporarily suspend Crosswork Network Controller operations for maintenance or restart activities and resume normal service. Maintenance mode provides a graceful shutdown for system updates and synchronizes application data before suspending services.

For more information about the maintenance mode, please refer to following:

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/cloud-systems-management/crosswork-infrastructure/7-2/AdminGuide/b-cisco-crosswork-admin-guide-7-2/g-vm-management/t-manage-maintenance-mode-settings.html

Follow the steps blow to confirm the maintenance mode is off. If not, disable the maintenance mode.

  1. Sign in to the dCloud and click "View" button (Note, the scenario name could be different).
  2. Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop (use VM Consoel), run Firefox on the Desktop. Click "CNC" in the bookmark and access CNC (https://[2001:db8:134::200]:30603). After the log in, dashboard is displayed.
  3. Go to Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode.
  4. If a popup already offers to turn maintenance mode off, accept it.

  5. If the Maintenance slider is On, drag it to Off.

  6. Wait. The applications need several minutes.

Result: The maintenance slider stays Off, the UI loads the normal home page.

docs.title: 1.3 Confirm CML labs are running
docs.text:
In this lab, two CML instances are connected via multiple external connecors. Rivew the network topology and familiarize with the connection.

Follow the steps below and confirm both CMLs are up and running.

  1. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for XR" in the bookmark.
  2. Confirm "5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6" scenario is running. If not, start the scenario.
  3. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for PCE" in the bookmark.
  4. Confirm "xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6" scenario is running. IF not, start the scenario.

Result: The lab is booted. CNC can reach the devices after the providers and the Data Gateway are healthy. You confirm that reachability in the next chapter.

docs.title: 1.4 Sync-from devices
docs.text:
A key component of CNC is Network Services Orchestrator (NSO). NSO holds devices configuration to an internal database called CDB. The device configuration and CDB must be in sync for CNC to execute the provisioning.

If there is a diff, the state is changed to "out-of-sync". Once that happens, execute "sync-from" in Device Management and sync the configuration beween CNC and the devices.

Follow the steops below and get familialize with the sync operation.

  1. Access CNC and go to Device Management > Network Devices
  2. Select all devices and choose Sync-from devices to NSO from Actions
  3. Go to Inventory Jobs and wait for the task to be completed
  4. Open NSO by clicking "NSO" button located in the top right.
  5. Just click "SSO Login" to login to NSO, no need to fill out username and password.

Result: All devices are synec to CNC. You are in the UI as yourself, and the controller is in normal operating mode.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Maintenance mode is Off.
  • Log in to CNC
  • The CML labs are booted.
  • All devices are synced

docs.title: 2. CNC management
docs.text:
Time: 50 minutes.

Objective: Confirm that CNC 7.2 is healthy enough for topology, inventory, traffic engineering, and service provisioning. You are reading the system, not rebuilding it.

The rest of the lab depends on three things:

Later work Depends on Topology and SR policies SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS and PCEP from the routers Inventory, alarms, interface counters Data Gateway collection jobs L3VPN and L2VPN provisioning NSO provider, devices in sync

docs.title: 2.1 Crosswork Summary and Crosswork Health
docs.text:
The health state of CNC can be verified by viewing Crosswork Manager. In this scenario, go through the Crosswork state and packages.

  1. From the main menu, go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Stay on the Crosswork Summary tab. Read the tiles for the cluster (or single VM), Platform Infrastructure, and the installed applications.
  3. Open System summary. Confirm the VM is up and that CPU, memory, and disk are not in a warning state.
  4. Open the Crosswork Health tab.
  5. For each of the following applications, open the tile and confirm the application (and its microservices) are Healthy or Running:
    • Platform Infrastructure
    • Optimization Engine
    • Service Health, if it is installed (chapter 8 uses it)
    • Element Management Functions
    • Active Topology
  6. Open Alarms or Events on an application tile only far enough to see whether anything is raised against the platform itself. Device alarms belong in chapter 4 and chapter 9.

Result: You can name the applications this lab uses and their health state.

docs.title: 2.2 Providers
docs.text:
Crosswork Network Controller components depend on external services, such as Cisco Crosswork Network Services Orchestrator (NSO) and Segment Routing Path Computation Element (SR-PCE), to perform operations like configuration modifications and segment routing path calculations. To manage access and facilitate information sharing among Crosswork Network Controller components, each external service must have a configured provider that belongs to a specific provider family (for example, NSO or SR-PCE).

For more information, refer to following.

https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/cloud-systems-management/crosswork-infrastructure/7-2/AdminGuide/b-cisco-crosswork-admin-guide-7-2/g-DLM/c-providers.html

Follow the steps below and confirm the provider.

  1. Go to Administration > Manage Provider Access.
  2. Find the SR-PCE provider that points at the PCE CML lab (xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6). Read reachability and the protocol state. You want the provider reachable, with the topology feed up.
  3. Find the NSO provider. NSO can be reachable from the top right menu.
  4. Open a provider only far enough to see the credential profile name. The profile is a pointer. The password stays in the profile store.

Result: SR-PCE and NSO are both reachable.

If SR-PCE is down, stop before chapter 3. If NSO is down, you can still walk topology and element management; wait until NSO is reachable before chapters 6 and 7.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Gateway and collection at a glance
docs.text:
Interface counters, inventory detail, syslog, and SNMP traps arrive through a Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG). This dCloud session may use a dedicated Data Gateway VM or the embedded collector on a single VM. Either way, devices must be attached and collection must be running.

  1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management. (cluster only)
  2. Confirm the gateway (or pool) is enrolled and administratively Up. (cluster only)
  3. Open the gateway and confirm the XR lab devices are attached to it. (cluster only)
  4. Open Administration > Collection Jobs (or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs, depending on the build).
  5. On Bulk jobs, confirm system jobs are READY or Successful, not Failed.

Result: You can point at the collector that feeds inventory, alarms, and utilization. You will read collection jobs in more detail in chapter 9.

docs.title: 2.4 What you leave alone
docs.text:
Credential profiles, AAA, certificates, backup jobs, and licensing are visible from Administration and from Device Management > Credential Profiles. Open a profile only if a device is unreachable and you need to compare the profile name.

Backup, restore, and Add OS patch put the cluster into maintenance mode. Patching is a guided walk in chapter 9. Do not start it here.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Platform Infrastructure, Optimization Engine, Active Topology, and element management are Healthy or Running.
  • The SR-PCE provider is reachable.
  • The NSO provider is reachable.
  • A Data Gateway (or embedded collector) is Up and the XR devices are attached.
  • Collection jobs are not in a Failed state.

docs.title: 3. Active Topology
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Use Crosswork Active Topology to answer where a device sits and how it is connected, then prove the same facts from IOS-XR CLI.

Active Topology is the map. Optimization Engine draws traffic-engineering objects on top of the same topology. You will use both views, then open a PE console from CML.

This lab is IPv6. IS-IS, BGP-LS, SRv6 locators, and PCEP should match what the map shows.

docs.title: 3.1 Open the map
docs.text:
1. From the main menu, open Topology.
  2. Wait for the devices from 5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6 to appear. An empty map usually means the SR-PCE provider is up and BGP-LS is still down, or the CML nodes are still booting. Recheck chapter 2.
  3. Routers are located on the geographic map based on the longitude/latitude configured in the Device Management.
  4. Identify three provider-edge routers. Those become the headend and the endpoint for chapters 5 through 8.

Result: You can find both PEs and at least one IGP path between them.

docs.title: 3.2 Read a device and a link in CNC
docs.text:
1. Select the headend. Open the Device details panel.
  2. Record hostname, management IPv6 address, reachability, and IGP router ID.
  3. Select a core link on a path between any router.
  4. In the link details, record:
    • Interface names on each side
    • IGP metric
    • TE metric
    • Utilization
  5. Switch the layer to Traffic Engineering and confirm SRv6 locators.

docs.title: 3.3 Confirm the same topology from XR CLI
docs.text: Open a new tab in Firefox and click "CML2 for XR" to access XR routers. Open a console on the headend PE. Stay in EXEC. Do not enter configuration mode.

docs.title: Neighbors and IGP
docs.text:
show isis neighbors
show isis ipv6 topology

If the lab uses a named IS-IS instance, the instructor will give you the instance name and you will use:

show isis instance <name> neighbors
show isis instance <name> ipv6 topology

Match each IS-IS neighbor to a node on the CNC map. The neighbor count and the path you traced in section 3.2 should agree.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
show ipv6 interface brief
show interface <core-interface> brief

Confirm the core interface you clicked on the map is up/up and that the IPv6 address matches the link panel in CNC.

docs.title: SRv6
docs.text:
show segment-routing srv6 locator
show segment-routing srv6 sid

The locator prefix on the PE should match the SRv6 layer on the map. If the map shows a locator and the CLI does not, the topology feed is stale. Wait and refresh; do not configure a locator.

docs.title: How CNC learned this topology
docs.text:
On the PE:

show bgp link-state link-state
show bgp link-state link-state summary

On the SR-PCE (the second CML lab), if the instructor opens that console:

show pce ipv6 peer
show pce ipv6 topology summary

PCE should list the PEs as BGP-LS and PCEP peers. That is the feed behind the CNC map.

Result: Hostname, neighbor, core interface, and SRv6 locator agree between CNC and CLI.

docs.title: 3.4 Dashboard baseline
docs.text:
1. Return to the home page or the topology dashboard.
  2. Record the reachable-device count and the SR policy count.
  3. Zero SR policies is acceptable before chapter 5. You will compare the policy count after you create a PCE-initiated policy.

Result: You have a baseline count of devices and policies.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Both lab PEs are on the map and reachable.
  • show isis neighbors (or the named-instance form) matches the map.
  • The core interface and SRv6 locator you recorded in CNC appear in XR CLI.
  • You know the baseline SR policy count.

docs.title: 4. Element management
docs.text:
Time: 50 minutes.

Objective: Use CNC Element Management Functions to manage node status, hardware inventory, configuration archive, alarms, and interface performance. Deploy nothing from this chapter.

Element Management Functions in CNC 7.2 cover device onboarding, inventory, faults, metrics, software images, configuration backup, and configuration templates.

docs.title: 4.1 Compare CNC to generic NMS (Network Management System)
docs.text:
CNC is the controller view of the same devices, with IGP and SR context. The following is the comparison between CNC and generic NMS.

Generic NMS CNC What is different Node list, ICMP/SNMP reachability Device Management > Network Devices CNC also shows the credential profile and the Data Gateway mapping that collection uses Hardware inventory (chassis, modules, serials) Device Management > Network Inventory Same idea: serial, product id, alarm badge on the part Network map Topology (chapter 3) CNC map is IGP/SRv6 from SR-PCE, not only Layer-3 discovery Alert console / trap viewer Alerts > Alarms and Events CNC splits system, network, and device alarms. An alarm stays until it clears; an event is a point in time Interface utilization and thresholds Device Management > Performance Policies, plus link utilization on the topology map CNC Optimization Engine colors links from collected counters. Performance Policies raise threshold-crossing alarms NCM config archive, compare, restore Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore CNC can also backup on configuration change. Restore is out of scope for this lab NCM config change jobs / scripts Device Management > Configuration Templates Parameterized CLI (Apache Velocity). Different from NSO L2/L3VPN templates in chapters 6 and 7

Use the table as a translation layer. The rest of this chapter is the CNC side.

docs.title: 4.2 Network devices and inventory
docs.text:
1. Go to Device Management > Network Devices.
  2. Find the headend from chapter 3. Record operational state, reachability, and the credential profile name.
  3. Go to Device Management > Network Inventory.
  4. Filter to the headend hostname or product family (C8711-1-PE).
  5. Open the chassis, one route processor or line card, and one pluggable if the inventory has them.
  6. Read the alarm summary on that inventory row.

Result: You can walk from a hostname to a chassis and a module.

A device that stays unreachable needs credentials, IPv6 reachability to the management address, and a booted CML node.

docs.title: 4.3 Configuration backup
docs.text:
CNC archives device configuration, compares two archives, and can restore. This lab uses the archive as a reader, like NCM config view.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore.
  2. Find the headend.
  3. Open the latest archived configuration. Identify hostname and the segment-routing or IS-IS section.
  4. If two archives exist, open compare and name one difference, or state that they match.
  5. Leave Schedule backup and Restore unused.

Result: You have seen a real archived configuration for the headend.

Automatic backup on configuration change, when it is enabled under Device Management > Configuration Preferences, is what makes this archive useful after chapters 6 and 7. Read the preference. Leave the values as you found them.

docs.title: 4.4 Configuration templates (read only)
docs.text:
Device templates under Device Management are parameterized CLI. They are for repeating underlay or day-1 configuration. They are not the NSO L2VPN/L3VPN function-pack templates, and they are not the custom template you may attach to a VPWS in chapter 7.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Templates.
  2. Open one existing template, if any exist. Read the device types it targets and one variable it expects.
  3. Configuration templates can be used to execute a set of commands. Create a new template and put following values.
    • Name: collect-outputs
    • Enable "Read template for troubleshooting"
    • Authorization: admin
  4. Select "Cisco 8711-32FH" as a device type.
  5. No input for Define variable, just click Next
  6. Put show commands in Configure template script
  7. Deploy created template
  8. Go to Jobs to see the progress.

docs.title: 4.5 Alarms and events
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Stay on Alarms. Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets.
  3. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it.
  4. If an alarm is present, record severity, source, and whether it is acknowledged. Leave acknowledge, clear, and annotate unused unless the instructor gives you a lab alarm of your own.
  5. Switch Show from Alarms to Events.
  6. Read the newest event. An event is a moment in time. An alarm remains until it clears.

Result: You can open both views. An empty alarm list is valid on a healthy CML lab.

You will use this page again in chapter 9.

docs.title: 4.6 Performance
docs.text:
Link colors on the topology map come from interface utilization collected for Optimization Engine. Element management adds polling policies.

  1. Go to Device Management > Performance Policies.
  2. Open one existing policy, if any exist. Read which devices it covers, how often it polls, and which threshold raises an alarm.
  3. Return to the Topology and click any link. Open History and confirm the utilization and traffic rate.
  4. Leave the policy switch as you found it.

Result: You can say where a threshold is defined, and you can point at one live counter.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can map node list, inventory, alerts, config archive, and utilization.
  • The headend is in Network Devices and in Network Inventory.
  • You opened an archived configuration and did not restore it.
  • You opened Alarms and Events.
  • You compared one interface counter with the topology utilization from chapter 3.

docs.title: 5. SR-TE and SRv6
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes.

Objective: Create valious PCE-initiated SRv6 policies from CNC.

Note

Cisco 8000 does not support SRv6 policies with head-end computed dynamic paths and PCE-initiated SRv6 policies. Also, the CNC 7.2 built-in function pack does not support explicit paths with IPv6 addresses/SRv6 SIDs. Therefore, this hands-on focuses on PCC-initiated SRv6 policies with PCE-delegated dynamic paths. For details, please visit Cisco 8000 Configuration Guide: Segment Routing over IPv6 Traffic Engineering (SRv6-TE)

docs.title: 5.1 Words you need
docs.text: Term Meaning in this lab PCC The headend router. It owns the policy configuration, and it has a PCEP session to SR-PCE. PCE SR-PCE in the second CML lab. It learns the topology through BGP-LS, computes paths, and reports the policies to CNC. PCC-initiated The policy configuration lives on the headend. In this lab, you create it in CNC, and CNC provisions the configuration on the headend through NSO. This is the type used in this chapter. PCE-delegated dynamic path A PCC-initiated candidate path with dynamic + pce. The headend delegates path computation to SR-PCE, and SR-PCE returns the SID list through PCEP. PCE-initiated The policy is created on SR-PCE and pushed to the headend through PCEP, with no configuration on the headend. Not used in this lab because Cisco 8000 does not support it for SRv6. Color A number that identifies the intent. Together with the endpoint, it identifies the policy. Chapter 6 binds an L3VPN to this color. Candidate path One way to reach the endpoint. Preference chooses among candidate paths.

docs.title: 5.2 Confirmation of initial state
docs.text:
SR-PCE requires topology and SRv6 Locator/SID information to perform path calculation. it acquires this information via BGP-LS from routers within the SRv6 topology. In this scenario, BGP-LS sessions are established with three PEs.

On the SR-PCE console:

PCEP (Path Computation Element Communication Protocol) is a signaling protocol for exchanging SRv6-TE path information between an SR-PCE that performs path computation and head-end routers (PCCs) in the network (RFC 5440).

PCEP handles bidirectional communication between routers and PCEs, including path computation requests (Request), instructions for computation results (Report/Update), and delegation of control (Delegation).

docs.title: 5.3 Create a PCE-initiated policy 1 (Exclude RED link)
docs.text:
Configure an SRv6-TE policy with the following conditions:

  • Policy Name: PE1_PE2_color10
  • Headend: PE1
  • Endpoint: PE2
  • Optimization: IGP
  • Constraint: exclude RED link

Since all links in this topology use default costs, in this case, the path from PE1 to PE2 should be calculated as follows, avoiding the link between P4 and PE2.

There are two methods available; please perform the configuration using either method. Option 1: Manually configure parameters Option 2: Import JSON

docs.title: Option 5-3-1: Manually configure parameters
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering, SRv6 tab, then click Create.

  2. Click + button.

  3. Set:

    • name: PE1-PE2_color10
    • headend: C8711-1-PE
    • endpoint: 2001:db8::2
    • color: 10
    • preference: 100
    • st-te-path-choice: dynamic-path (Enable dynamic and Check pce)
    • metric-type: igp
    • contraints: enable affinity and add a rule with an action exclude-any color RED.
    • srv6: enable locator (locator-name: srv6, behavior: ub6-insert-reduced, and binding-sid-type: srv6-dynamic).

  4. Dry-run to confirm the configuration.

    You can switch the display with Show changes on the upper right.

  5. Commit changes

docs.title: Option 5-3-2: Import JSON
docs.text:
You can also configure it by loading a JSON file. The sample JSON files are exported from the following.

This time, we will load the JSON file prepared in advance using the procedure below.

  1. Open the terminal and clone the JSON file repository from git.

    git clone https://github.com/mekawaba/cnc-payloads.git

  2. Load Home > cnc-payloads > PE1-PE2_color10.json.

    PE1-PE2_color10.json 
    {
    "cisco-sr-te-cfp:sr-te": {
      "cisco-sr-te-cfp-sr-policies:policies": {
        "policy": [
          {
            "name": "PE1-PE2_color10",
            "head-end": [
              {
                "name": "C8711-1-PE"
              }
            ],
            "srv6": {
              "locator": {
                "locator-name": "srv6",
                "behavior": "ub6-insert-reduced",
                "binding-sid-type": "srv6-dynamic"

docs.title: 6.5 Packet Capture (Option)
docs.text:
We will use the packet capture feature of CML to observe the encapsulation in an IPv6 header.

  1. Start ping to the CE-facing interface address of PE2 at PE1. 

    RP/0/RP0/CPU0:C8711-1-PE# ping vrf CustA 192.168.2.1 count 100000

  2. Right click the link between P4 and PE2

  3. Start a packet capture.

  4. Click the ICMP echo from 192.168.1.1 to 192.168.2.1.

  5. Find the IPv6 header. The destination address should be the PE2 uDT4 (ex. fcbb:bb00:2:e002::).

docs.title: 7. L2VPN provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes for VPWS. Optional sections add about 30 minutes.

Objective: Provision a point-to-point L2VPN (VPWS) and a multipoint LAN (VPLS) from CNC.

docs.title: 7.1 VPWS
docs.text:
CNC 7.2 provisions IETF L2VPN network models through NSO. VPWS is a wire between two attachment circuits.

Field Value Service name CustD_vpws vpn-type point-to-point (vpws-evpn) Endpoints PE1, PE2 Transport SRv6, steering to SRv6 Policy with color 10

docs.title: 7.1.1 Pre-check (ID-Pools)
docs.text:
EVI IDs and Source/Target IDs can be automatically assigned from predefined pools. It is also possible to set fixed values.

In this instance, we will confirm that those pools are already configured.

  1. Resource Pools (the range of assignable values) are located under Global > Resource Pool.

    • evi-id-pool: Pool for EVI IDs
    • evi-source-target-pool: Pool for Source/Target IDs

    By clicking Edit under Actions, you can see that the following values are set for each. Please close with Cancel after confirmation.

    • evi-id-pool: 100-500
    • evi-source-target-pool: 1-100

  2. Confirm that these pools are used in the L2VPN configuration under L2VPN > ID-Pools.

    • evi-id-pool-name: evi-id-pool
    • evi-source-target-pool-name: evi-source-target-pool

docs.title: 7.1.2 Pre-configuration (CEs)
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO).
  2. Open the L2VPN service type.
  3. Create a service named vpws-01.
  4. Set vpn-id to a unique value the instructor assigns.
  5. Set vpn-type to the point-to-point / VPWS choice. Do not choose a multipoint or VPLS type here. If the form only lists mpls-evpn when you add more than two vpn-nodes, you have the wrong number of endpoints. VPWS uses two.
  6. Add two vpn-nodes. For each node set the device and the attachment circuit (interface, VLAN if the instructor specified one).
  7. Set underlay transport to SRv6. If preferred-path or ODN is offered, bind it the way the instructor specified. Preferred path onto pce-01 is the consistent choice with chapter 6.
  8. Leave Custom-template empty for the required service. Optional section 7.3 uses that field on a copy, not on this one.
  9. Run Dry run. Confirm the service name, two endpoints, and vpn-type. Confirm it is not a VPLS.
  10. Commit.
  11. Open the service. Confirm it is in sync.

Result: vpws-01 is committed and in sync.

docs.title: 7.2 Visualize and confirm from CLI
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services.
  2. Select vpws-01. Show it on the map. You should see a point-to-point overlay between the two PEs, not a multipoint LAN.
  3. On the headend:
show l2vpn xconnect
show l2vpn xconnect detail

Find the xconnect NSO created. Attachment circuit and pseudowire (or SRv6 EVPN VPWS equivalent) should be up. If the lab uses EVPN VPWS, the instructor may also ask for:

show l2vpn evpn xconnect
show bgp l2vpn evpn summary

Use the form that actually prints your service. Leave configuration mode.

Result: The map is point-to-point, and XR shows the xconnect up.

docs.title: 7.3 Optional: VPLS
docs.text:
Do this section only if the instructor asks for it. Chapter 8 does not enable Service Health on a VPLS.

  1. In Provisioning (NSO), create a second L2VPN named vpls-01.
  2. Choose the VPLS or multipoint vpn-type the form offers. Add at least two vpn-nodes (three if the instructor wants a true multipoint picture).
  3. Dry run, then commit.
  4. In VPN Services, select vpls-01 and confirm the overlay is multipoint.
  5. On a PE:
show l2vpn bridge-domain

Use this only to contrast with show l2vpn xconnect from the VPWS. Delete vpls-01 before the end of the day if you created it. Do not start Service Health on it.

Result: You can tell VPWS (xconnect) from VPLS (bridge-domain) in both CNC and CLI.

docs.title: 7.4 Optional: NSO custom template
docs.text:
An NSO custom template adds CLI that the L2VPN function pack does not model (for example an extra QoS or interface command). Templates must already exist in NSO. CNC only displays parameterizable fields.

  1. Ask the instructor for the template name, if one is loaded.
  2. Open vpws-01 in edit, or clone it to vpws-template-01 if you should not change the monitored service.
  3. In Custom-template, select the template. Fill the variables CNC shows.
  4. Dry run. Read the extra CLI the template adds.
  5. Commit only if the instructor wants the extra CLI on the device.
  6. If you only needed to see the fields, cancel without commit.

This is not a Device Management configuration template from chapter 4.

Result: You saw how a custom template attaches to a VPWS, and you know which store it lives in.

docs.title: 7.5 Optional: sync-from
docs.text:
NSO keeps a copy of device configuration. Check sync compares that copy with the device. Sync from pulls the device configuration into NSO. Sync to pushes NSO to the device. Redeploy reconcile rebuilds the service while keeping non-service configuration.

Use this on the VPWS only when the instructor wants the room to see out-of-sync handling. sync-from after a service commit can make the service look out of sync until you redeploy. That is the lesson, and it is easy to leave messy.

  1. On vpws-01, open Actions.
  2. Run Check sync. Record in-sync or out-of-sync.
  3. Open Config view or View in NSO and read the service data.
  4. If the instructor has made a small out-of-band change on one PE, run Sync from.
  5. Run Check sync again. Expect out-of-sync if the device now differs from the service model.
  6. Run Redeploy dry run, then Redeploy reconcile only if the instructor wants the service model to win.

Do not run Sync to unless the instructor says so. Sync to overwrites the device with NSO's copy.

Result: You can say what Check sync, Sync from, Sync to, and Redeploy reconcile each do, and you used only the actions the instructor approved.

docs.title: 7.6 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep vpws-01 through chapter 8. Delete optional VPLS and template clones first at the end of the day, then the VPWS, then the L3VPN, then the PCE-initiated policy.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• vpws-01 is in sync and shown as point-to-point in VPN Services.
  • show l2vpn xconnect (or the EVPN form) lists the service.
  • Optional sections are either completed or marked skipped.

docs.title: 8. Assurance
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes.

Objective: Enable CNC Service Health on the VPWS from chapter 7 and read Basic monitoring until the health column has a real state. Do not monitor VPLS.

Service Health scores a provisioned VPN against heuristic rules. For L2VPN it looks at VPWS xconnect state, device CPU and memory, and, in Advanced mode, interfaces, PCEP, SR policy, and path reachability. This lab uses Basic Monitoring on vpws-01 only.

docs.title: 8.1 Find the VPWS
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services.
  2. Select vpws-01.
  3. Confirm vpn-type is point-to-point / VPWS. If you also created vpls-01 in chapter 7, leave it unmonitored.
  4. Confirm the service is in sync. Service Health on an out-of-sync service is not a useful baseline. Fix sync in chapter 7 before you start monitoring.

Result: You are looking at the VPWS, not the L3VPN and not a VPLS.

docs.title: 8.2 Start Basic monitoring
docs.text:
1. In the Actions menu for vpws-01, choose Start monitoring.
  2. Set monitoring level to Basic Monitoring. Do not choose Advanced unless the instructor wants the extra subservices and you have time to wait. Switching levels can take more than 15 minutes before symptoms appear.
  3. Select the configuration profile the instructor names (often a Gold or Silver heuristic profile that is already loaded).
  4. Start monitoring.
  5. Wait. The Health column moves from Initiated to Good, Degraded, Down, or Not Monitoring.

Result: Health is no longer empty.

If Health stays on Initiated, collection for Service Health is still starting. Parameterized collection jobs of type service-based appear under Administration > Collection Jobs. You will read those jobs in chapter 9. Give Basic monitoring several minutes on this lab.

docs.title: 8.3 Read the health of the VPWS
docs.text:
1. Open vpws-01.
  2. Read the Health state and the list of subservices. For Basic L2VPN / VPWS, expect rules that cover:
    • VPWS xconnect / control-plane health
    • Device health (CPU, memory)
    • ODN or SR policy health, if the service is bound to a policy
  3. Open one subservice. Read the metric that is Good or Degraded. Typical metrics are xconnect.state, attachment-circuit state, and pseudowire state.
  4. If Health is Degraded or Down, do not clear anything yet. Note the symptom, then confirm it on the PE:
show l2vpn xconnect
show l2vpn xconnect detail

A down attachment circuit on the router should match a down AC metric in Service Health. If CNC says Down and XR says Up, wait for the next collection cycle, then look at collection jobs in chapter 9.

  1. On the map, with the VPWS selected, confirm the overlay still terminates on the two PEs you provisioned.

Result: You can point at the heuristic result and at the matching XR xconnect state.

docs.title: 8.4 What you do not do in this chapter
docs.text:
• Do not start monitoring on vpls-01 or on any multipoint L2VPN.
  • Do not start monitoring on l3vpn-01 unless the instructor adds it as extra credit. The required assurance object is the VPWS.
  • Do not switch this VPWS to Advanced Monitoring after Basic has already started, unless the instructor wants to show the delay.
  • Do not stop monitoring until the instructor says the chapter is done. Stopping with "retain historical data" is available; use it only if you need to restart.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Service Health is running on vpws-01 at Basic Monitoring.
  • You can name the Health state and one subservice or metric.
  • That metric agrees with show l2vpn xconnect (or you have recorded a collection lag).
  • No VPLS is being monitored.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Collect CNC showtech, read collection jobs, read alarms, and walk the add-patch workflow. Applying a patch is an instructor decision because CNC puts itself into maintenance mode to install it.

This chapter is about the controller, not about rewriting router configuration.

docs.title: 9.1 Alarms
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Filter Alarms by category: system, network, and device.
  3. For each category, record whether anything is raised. System alarms belong to CNC itself (disk, application, collector). Device alarms belong to the XR nodes.
  4. Open one alarm if any exist. Record severity, source, time, and description. Leave acknowledge and clear unused unless the instructor assigns that alarm to you.
  5. Switch to Events and find the event that created the alarm, if one exists.

Result: You know whether the platform, the network, or a device is currently unhappy.

Use alarms together with chapter 2 health tiles. A Healthy application tile and a system alarm can both be true; the alarm is the detail.

docs.title: 9.2 Collection jobs
docs.text:
Empty inventory, blank utilization, and Service Health stuck on Initiated are usually collection problems, not VPN problems.

  1. Go to Administration > Collection Jobs, or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs.
  2. Open Bulk jobs. These are created by the system, the UI, or the API. Record Status (Successful etc.) and Context id.

  3. Open a successful job and read the device names.

  4. Go through the details of Job Monitoring.

  5. If a job is Degraded, open the job details and read the error. Common causes:

    • Device not attached to a Data Gateway
    • SNMP or CLI credentials wrong
    • Device unreachable (chapter 3 CLI will already have shown this)
    • Destination in Error, while collection still runs and increments an error count

  6. Explore the job distribution details, understand the difference between Collection and Distribution.

Result: You can point at the jobs and their status.

docs.title: 9.3 Showtech
docs.text: Showtech is what you collect before you open a TAC case. CNC 7.2 collects cluster logs and metrics from Crosswork Manager. Application showtech is per application. Data Gateway showtech is a separate encrypted download.

docs.title: Cluster and application
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open Crosswork Summary > System summary.
  3. Click Actions and note the showtech options:
    • Request all — logs and metrics
    • Request metrics
    • Request logs
  4. If the instructor wants a file from this VM, collect logs (not Request all) so the bundle stays smaller. Otherwise, only open Actions > View showtech jobs and read any previous job.
  5. To collect for one application, return to Crosswork Health, open the application tile (for example Service Health or Platform Infrastructure), and use that tile's showtech action. Application logs are collected separately from the cluster bundle.
  6. In View showtech jobs, read status. Publish or download only if the instructor will take the file. Delete nothing.

Result: You know where cluster showtech and application showtech are started, and you did not fill the disk unless the instructor asked for a collect.

docs.title: Data Gateway (for cluster only)
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management.
  2. Select the gateway.
  3. Open Actions and find Download Showtech.
  4. Do not download unless the instructor asks. The file is encrypted. The instructor keeps the passphrase and decrypts the file if TAC needs it. Do not put a passphrase in chat or in this guide.

Result: You can show where CDG showtech lives.

docs.title: 9.4 Add patch
docs.text: CNC 7.2 installs OS security patches (SPACK) from System management. Application bundles are added from Application Management. Both are maintenance operations. Adding an OS patch automatically turns maintenance mode on, applies the bundle node by node, and turns maintenance mode off. Rollback is not supported. A small lab VM still takes a long time.

docs.title: OS patch screens
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open the System management tab.
  3. Find Add OS patch. Open the dialog far enough to see that the source is URL or SCP.
  4. Open System updates (or the list of already installed patches). Record whether this dCloud image already shows 7.2.0.
  5. Open Job History on System management. This is where add-to-repository and per-VM apply jobs appear after someone adds a patch. Read any existing job. Do not retry a job unless the instructor is recovering a failed apply.
  6. After a successful apply (instructor only), verification is Administration > Crosswork Manager > System summary > Package details.

docs.title: Application file
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager > Application Management.
  2. Note Add new file. That is how an application CAPP or a patch bundle is uploaded.
  3. Do not upload a file unless the instructor provides one and asks you to.

docs.title: 9.5 If something from an earlier chapter is still broken
docs.text: Symptom First check Empty topology SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS, show pce ipv6 topology summary Device unreachable in Network Devices CML node booted, management IPv6, credential profile Thin inventory / no utilization Data Gateway attachment, collection job status SR policy preview empty SRv6 tab, show segment-routing srv6 locator, PCEP peer VPN out of sync NSO provider, Check sync, then chapter 7 optional sync-from only if asked Service Health stuck on Initiated Parameterized service-based collection job

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You opened Alarms and Events and recorded what is (or is not) raised.
  • You found bulk and parameterized collection jobs, including a service-based job for the VPWS when monitoring is on.
  • You can start cluster showtech from System summary and you know that application and CDG showtech are separate.
  • You walked Add OS patch and Job History without starting an unplanned maintenance window.

docs.title: . Optional: CNC MCP server
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes

Objective: Ask the lab assistant one question that it can answer with a live Crosswork tool. Confirm the answer in the CNC UI.The assistant is a chat page. When you ask a question, it may call tools on an MCP server. That server is what talks to CNC.

docs.title: 10.1 Open the assistant
docs.text:
Access Ubuntu2504-Desktop, open Terminal and execute following: 

$ cd aiserver
$ ./main
Close the browser tab.

Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop, open terminal and execute following: 

$ cd cnc_mcp
$ source venv/bin/activate
$ python3 cnc_mcp_server2.py

Open another terminal in Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop and execute following: 

$ cd webui
$ source venv/bin/actiate
$ streamlit run frontend.py

Result: The assistant is online and you can name the Tools.

docs.title: 10.2 One live question
docs.text:
In the chat, ask:

How many nodes are in the CNC?

Wait for the reply. Open the tool-call detail for that turn.

Check all of the following:

  • The assistant called the inventory count tool.
  • The reply contains a number.
  • You can find a matching count under Device Management > Network Devices or Network Inventory. The two screens group equipment differently, so the numbers may differ by what each one counts. Write both numbers and one sentence on the difference. If they match, write that they match.

If the tool call fails, the useful symptom is the error text, not a second guess from the model. A failure here usually means the assistant cannot authenticate to CNC or cannot reach the UI address. That is an instructor fix. Chapters 2 and 4 already showed you the same inventory with your own login.

Result: A number from the tool, compared with Device Management.

docs.title: 10.3 Operator check, not a write
docs.text:
Ask a second question that does not require a write tool:

The inventory count is <the number you just verified>.
What should an operator check first in Crosswork?

A useful answer names checks you already know how to open:

  • Reachability on Device Management > Network Devices
  • The credential profile on that device
  • Data Gateway mapping
  • Collection job status
  • SR-PCE and NSO provider status
  • Active alarms for that hostname

Take one check the assistant named, open that CNC page, and confirm or contradict the suggestion with the screen. The screen wins.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text: • The assistant answered the inventory question with a tool call, and you compared that number with Device Management.
